title: The ‘devil’s interval’ was never actually banned by the Church
body: The tritone, three whole tones such as F to B, splits the octave exactly in half and sounds restless and unresolved, so medieval and Renaissance theorists treated it as unstable and avoided it; Guido of Arezzo’s hexachord system was built partly to sidestep the F–B clash. Writers in the 1720s and 1730s passed on its nickname **diabolus in musica**, the devil in music. But stories of singers being excommunicated or punished by the Church for using it are likely fanciful: it was a rule of good style, not law. Today the devil is everywhere, from the opening of West Side Story to jazz, where tritone substitution is one of the most common tricks.

left.label: Myth
left.text: The medieval Church banned the tritone and punished singers who dared to use it.

right.label: Record
right.text: Theorists avoided it as unstable, and 18th-century writers called it the devil in music. Tales of punishment are likely fanciful.

slides.heading: What is a tritone?
slides.text: Six semitones, exactly half an octave in equal temperament: play F and the B above it. Written as an augmented fourth or a diminished fifth, it pulls strongly towards resolution, which is why composers reach for it to build tension.

slides.heading: Intervals from a C, in semitones
slides.note: Six semitones split the twelve of an octave exactly in half.

slides.heading: The jazz devil
slides.text: In jazz the tritone sits inside the dominant chord and inside its substitute: two dominant chords a tritone apart share the same tritone, so one can stand in for the other. This tritone substitution is one of the most common devices in jazz.

slides.heading: Which interval is not a tritone?
slides.explanation: F–B, C–F♯ and B–F each span six semitones, half an octave. C to G is a perfect fifth, seven semitones.

slides.question: Which show’s opening Prologue begins with a tritone, as writer Timothy Judd points out?
slides.explanation: Leonard Bernstein used the tritone as a basis for much of West Side Story: it is the first interval in the Prologue and returns in ‘Maria’ and ‘Cool’.
